items.title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
items.abstract: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.

items.title: SCIENTIFIC SUBSTANTIATION OF ENSURING THE QUALITY OF NURSING CARE IN SURGICAL DEPARTMENTS OF EMERGENCY MEDICAL CARE CENTERS: AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY
items.abstract: Highlight: Surgical department nurses working in Uzbekistan's emergency-care system show markedly elevated, task-dependent occupational morbidity and a high prevalence of burnout that correlate with measurable deficits in workload allocation and organisational quality, pointing to concrete, evidence-based levers for improving nursing-care quality. Surgical nursing care is a core component of emergency medical services, yet the workload, morbidity, occupational strain and quality determinants of nurses working in surgical departments of emergency care centers remain insufficiently studied, particularly in Central Asia, motivating a study to scientifically substantiate measures for improving the professional competence, quality and effectiveness of the work of surgical department nurses (SDNs) at a Republican Scientific Center of Emergency Medical Care (RSCEMC) and its regional branches. A multi-stage cross-sectional study was conducted at the RSCEMC and its Farg'ona, Sirdaryo and Khorazm branches, involving 532 SDNs (309 ward, 122 treatment-room and 101 dressing-room/operating nurses), 143 surgical physicians, and 579 patients (1254 participants in total), selected by cluster and random sampling, using analysis of three-year morbidity records (2019-2021), a socio-hygienic lifestyle questionnaire, chronometry of working time (36 nurses, 360 working days, 2340 hours), the Maslach Burnout Inventory (Vodopyanova adaptation) for emotional strain, structured expert evaluation by senior physicians and head nurses, and physician/patient satisfaction surveys. Overall nurse morbidity was 1022.5 per 1000 nurses (ward 990.2; treatment-room 968.3; operating 1105.0), rising with age and tenure (r=0.68); five disease classes accounted for 73.4-86.3% of all morbidity, with operating nurses showing 1.6-1.7 times more nervous-system and 6-8 times more musculoskeletal disease than other nurses. Chronometry showed nurses spent 29.4-50.0% of working time executing physician orders and 23.9-29.4% on documentation, leaving only about one-fifth of ward nurses' time for direct patient care. High-level emotional strain was found in 45.7% of SDNs overall (51.6% of operating nurses), correlated with length of service (r=0.264, p<0.05). Expert evaluation showed markedly better workplace organisation, documentation, physician-order compliance, infection-control adherence and ethics compliance at the central RSCEMC than at its branches. Physician satisfaction correlated strongly with timely and complete execution of orders (r=0.89-0.91) and clinical vigilance (r=0.85); patient satisfaction (76.7-81.0% across nurse groups) correlated with prompt clinical responsiveness (r=0.63) and use of modern technology (r=0.53). Nursing care quality in surgical departments of emergency centers is accordingly shaped by an interacting set of occupational-health, workload, competency and organisational factors; targeted health protection, workload redistribution, and regular expert and patient-satisfaction monitoring are needed to improve the quality and effectiveness of surgical nursing care.

items.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
items.abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

items.title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
items.abstract: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.

items.title: Self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms among airport employees across multiple occupational groups: a European cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Objectives. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a significant challenge for companies around the globe, including airport environments. Airport studies are limited and have mostly focused on specific occupational groups, particularly baggage handlers, without considering the whole airport community. The aim of this study was to investigate self-reported musculoskeletal symptoms among airport employees across multiple occupational groups. Methods. This cross-sectional study utilized an adapted version of the Nordic musculoskeletal questionnaire (NMQ) with a pain intensity scale. The study was open to every airport employee from 35 companies who agreed to participate; 847 participants fulfilled the inclusion criteria. In addition, a focus group with seven health and safety (H&S) practitioners and three one-to-one email interviews were conducted. The qualitative data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis (RTA). Results. The most common 12-month prevalence rates were for the neck (49.7%), lower back (47.7%) and shoulder pain (45.7%). Additionally, the results showed that females reported higher symptom prevalence and pain intensity than males. Conclusions. Airport employees’ well-being may be improved through tailored ergonomic interventions, occupation-specific risk assessments, employee education and occupational health support.

items.abstract: SIEGE-1 / SIEGE-1R / SIEGE-2 — the Long Siege battery: six years of simulated attacker evolution thrown at the PORTCULLIS deterministic gate, escalating quantum-capability assumptions each wave (HNDL 2026, NISQ 2027, early fault-tolerance 2028, CRQC-early 2029, full CRQC 2030, CRQC-at-scale 2031), 79+ deterministic adjudications, no LLM in the decision path, preregistration-before-execution. Headline finding: across all six simulated years, no attack derived advantage from quantum capability itself. The gate's PQC material (kyber_1024, CRYSTALS-Dilithium3, SPHINCS+-256f) has no classical residue to break. Every CRQC-era success exploited PRE-QUANTUM trust seams: (C1) the gate trusted a claimed submitter string with no envelope binding; (C2) the pending-ACK queue was shared across submitters, allowing cross-tenant denial of the owner; (C3) the algorithm-role wall was one-directional (signature-class algorithms accepted for KEM-class operations); (C4) per-submitter budgets were trivially evaded by identity rotation. Hardening arc: SIP-030 approved, PORTCULLIS v1.4 built (amendments 10-13: envelope-bound submitter proof, owner-reserved ACK queue with per-submitter caps, bidirectional role wall, aggregate window cap). SIEGE-2 verification: PASS — C1 CLOSED, C2 CLOSED, C3 CLOSED, C4 BOUNDED; regression stayed closed; 4/4 owner controls admitted. Honest disclosures (append-only doctrine): SIEGE-1 run 1 suffered a harness defect (attacker budget exhaustion masked mid-wave seams) — kept unaltered, re-run corrected with fresh identities. SIEGE-2 run 1 flagged FAIL from harness predicate bugs while the gate's verdict column was correct throughout. SIEGE-2 also caught a REAL defect in v1.4 itself before deploy: the original aggregate cap (500) was unreachable in a 250-record window — dead code — reparameterized to 125 and disclosed. items.title: Single-cell morpho-molecular foundation modeling from histopathology with PAST
items.abstract: We present PAST, a single-cell morpho-molecular foundation model trained on ~20 million paired single-cell image–transcriptome instances derived from 49 tissue sections, comprising 42 human sections from 40 independent patients and 7 mouse sections across 15 tumor and tissue contexts. By jointly encoding cellular morphology and gene expression, PAST learns unified cross-modal representations that capture both spatial and molecular heterogeneity at the cellular level, enabling accurate prediction of single-cell gene expression, virtual molecular staining, and multimodal survival analysis directly from routine pathology slides.

items.title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
items.abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human-like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human-verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.

items.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
items.abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

items.title: Sustainable and Green Networking: Architectures, Techniques, and Future Directions for Energy-Efficient Communication Infrastructures
items.abstract: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure is rapidly becoming an electrical energy consumer, and an increasingly non-trivial emitter of greenhouse-gases as a result of the growth of global data traffic, cloud computing, artificial-intelligence workloads and always-connected Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices. Sustainable and Green Networking tackles this challenge by building energy-awareness into the design, deployment and operation of communication networks without affecting performance, reliability and quality of service. This paper summarizes the key concepts of green networking derived from literature published from 2022 to 2025, outlines the major classes of energy-saving techniques (standby and sleep modes, rate adaptation, energy-proportional computing, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV) based orchestration, and renewable-powered infrastructure) and suggests a cross-layer conceptual framework that brings these techniques together under a single carbon-intensity feedback loop. As examples of application areas, green 5G/6G radio access networks, sustainable data centers, and energy efficient IoT/edge computing are presented. A comparative study of the energy savings potential reported in the recent literature is presented, followed by a discussion of open challenges in the research field: the performance-energy trade-off, the standardization of energy information exposure, and the AI/ML energy-overhead trade-off, as well as interesting future research directions: the standardization of energy information exposure and the AI-native energy orchestration. The results will inform researchers, network operators and policymakers in their quest for more sustainable digital infrastructures.

items.title: Sustainable Creative Talent Development through Work-Integrated Learning and Industry Engagement
items.abstract: Malaysia’s applied creative arts and media sector is being reshaped by digitalisation, project-based work, and changing industry expectations. However, higher education programmes do not always prepare graduates with the combination of creative, technical, digital, interpersonal, and professional competencies required by the industry. Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) can help address this gap by connecting academic learning with authentic workplace experiences. Nevertheless, WIL in creative arts education is often implemented as a short-term placement rather than as an integrated part of the curriculum. This conceptual paper proposes a stakeholder-informed WIL framework for sustainable creative talent development in Malaysia’s applied creative arts ecosystem. The framework is grounded in Experiential Learning Theory and organised using an Input–Process–Output structure. The inputs consist of industry-required competencies and active industry engagement. The process comprises structured WIL activities, including real-world projects, workplace exposure, industry mentorship, practitioner feedback, reflective learning, and curriculum collaboration. The intended outcomes are stronger employability skills, industry readiness, career adaptability, and sustainable creative talent development. The paper argues that effective WIL requires continuous collaboration among higher education institutions, students, industry practitioners, and policymakers. Its main conceptual contribution is the integration of competency requirements, industry participation, experiential learning, and graduate outcomes within a single framework designed for Malaysia’s applied creative arts sector. The framework offers practical guidance for improving curriculum relevance, clarifying stakeholder responsibilities, strengthening university–industry collaboration, and designing meaningful workplace learning experiences. Ultimately, it provides a foundation for developing adaptable, digitally capable, and future-ready creative graduates who can contribute to Malaysia’s evolving creative economy.

items.title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
items.abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. We present Symbolic Constraint Agents (SCA), a framework that mines symbolic constraints from API documentation, refines them against execution traces, and checks the agent's tool calls with an SMT solver at runtime. A violation triggers a natural-language warning or, when the valid replacement is uniquely determined, an automatic repair. On AppWorld, refinement raises error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on GPT-5.5 traces and from 39.3 to 61.9 on Qwen3.5-27B traces. At runtime, repair raises GPT-5.4-mini's task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call budget and 9.8 points when environment errors are hidden, while removing 59--87\% of failed calls across models, and transfers to $τ^2$-bench with gains of up to 5.6 points. These findings show that automatically acquired symbolic constraints can improve tool-calling reliability and task completion, particularly when failures are costly or difficult to diagnose.

items.title: Synthetic corroboration: when AI interpretation looks like independent evidence
items.abstract: People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. items.title: Syntropic Horizons of Hope — Conscience, Obligation, and Answerable Action
items.abstract: Human responsibility cannot be reduced either to compliance with established obligations or to fidelity to personal conviction. Both individuals and institutions can recognize genuine demands of responsibility, and both can misunderstand the realities to which they respond. This essay develops a philosophy of syntropic praxis in which conscience is understood as a situated, fallible, and cultivable capacity for recognition and judgment. Its exercise depends on disciplined attention, public inquiry, legitimate authority, the claims of others, and responsiveness to consequences. Through encounters with fallibilism, social epistemology, practical wisdom, conscientious objection, civil resistance, epistemic injustice, and artificial intelligence, the essay argues that corrigibility must be cultivated personally and organized institutionally. Syntropic praxis names neither a privileged form of conduct nor a guarantee of moral truth, but an orientation toward more coherent, justifiable, and responsible participation in shared reality.

items.title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
items.abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. Qwen3-0.6B has been fine-tuned with LoRA on Reason-9k and Bitext reply rows. JevBench accuracy shows no statistically significant change (55.4% to 54.5%, p=0.87), while expected calibration error falls from 0.292 to 0.169. Held-out Bitext routing accuracy reaches 98.3%. Cache reuse saves 15-37% of latency on an Apple M4 Pro, with token-identical replies in the FP32 demonstration cases. Scoring options on copies of the prompt cache matches full-sequence scoring to within 1.4e-6 in probability. Adding dialogue, industry and complaint data (System X+) improves support-task results but lowers IFEval accuracy from 55.5% to 45.0%. System X v4 uses Qwen3-1.7B, rebalanced data and teacher-rewritten reply targets. Against its base LLM, JevBench accuracy rises from 55.0% to 61.0% (p=0.04), with no statistically significant IFEval change (p=0.71). A matched latency test on unadapted Qwen3-1.7B saves 17-39%. One LLM judge prefers v4 replies to an unadapted 1.7B second call (31 to 11 pairs, p=0.003); the other's preference is not significant. These reply comparisons also differ in prompts and generation limits. State conflicts and unsupported reply details remain failure modes. Further studies with several seeds, human raters and real support data are recommended.

items.title: Systematic Review of AI-Based PHM Frameworks for Ship Systems and Equipment
items.abstract: Maritime operations require high levels of availability and safety under changing cargo, operational, and environmental conditions. Therefore, anticipating degradation and failures in critical ship systems is an important operational requirement.Although predictive maintenance has advanced rapidly through data-driven approaches and artificial intelligence (AI), the available literature remains fragmented and does not consistently establish the relationships among the ship systems analyzed, the methodological approaches employed, and the conditions required for operational implementation.This article presents a systematic literature review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to examine the development of AI-based predictive maintenance for ship systems from a Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) perspective. Scopus and Web of Science were searched, and predefined screening, eligibility, inclusion, and exclusion criteria were applied.The findings show that research is strongly concentrated on propulsion systems, classified under Ship Work Breakdown Structure (SWBS) Group 200, and electric-plant systems, classified under SWBS Group 300, with most studies focusing on detection and diagnosis. Prognostic and prescriptive applications remain comparatively less developed. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by machine-learning and deep-learning approaches using operational and condition-monitoring variables associated with different operating regimes.Overall, maritime PHM exhibits uneven levels of functional and implementation maturity. Important challenges remain in model comparability, independent validation, and sustained onboard deployment, while opportunities persist for extending PHM to underrepresented ship systems and validating these approaches in real-world fleet operations

items.title: Teaching critical thinking with artificial intelligence: An information literacy training model at the Library of the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing, Universitas Gadjah Mada
items.abstract: Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

items.title: The AI gaze and imagined places: Co-creation and negotiation with the generative AI assemblage
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

items.title: The Bargaining-Verification Trap in AI-Mediated Work: An Integrated Theory of Productivity, Worker Voice, and Organisational Resilience
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.

items.title: The Changing Architecture of Intellectual Property in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

items.abstract: This technofidele and political-scientific essay deconstructs how generative AI infrastructure weaponizes human vulnerabilities for mass behavioral manipulation. items.title: The Effect of Digital Leadership and Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Behavior: An Analysis of Ceo Discourses
items.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

items.title: THE EFFECT OF SAFETY CULTURE AND MANAGEMENT COMMITMENT ON THE EFFECTIVENESS OF THE OCCUPATIONAL HEALTH AND SAFETY (OHS) PROGRAM AT PERTAMINA REGIONAL 4 ZONE 11 FIELD CEPU
items.abstract: This study employed a quantitative associative approach with descriptive and verificative methods. The population consisted of 152 employees at Pertamina Regional 4 Zone 11 Field Cepu, and a sample of 60 respondents was selected using simple random sampling based on Slovin’s formula with a 10% margin of error. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using IBM SPSS 25, covering validity and reliability tests, classical assumption tests, simple linear regression, multiple linear regression, t-test, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination (R2). The results show that safety culture, management commitment, and OHS program effectiveness were all in the very good category, with mean scores of 4.60, 4.55, and 4.55, respectively. Hypothesis testing confirmed that safety culture has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₁ accepted; p = 0.000; R2 = 41.4). Management commitment also has a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₂ accepted; p = 0.012; R2 = 68.2). Simultaneously, safety culture and management commitment have a positive and significant effect on OHS program effectiveness (H₃ accepted; F count = 61.667 > F table= 3.16; sig = 0.000; R2 = 91.9%). The multiple regression equation obtained was Y = 24.619 + 0.783X1 + 1.111X2. Management commitment exerts a relatively stronger influence than safety culture on OHS program effectiveness. In conclusion, strengthening safety culture and management commitment is essential for improving OHS program effectiveness at CPP Gundih toward the sustainable achievement of zero-accident and zero-fatality targets.

items.title: The Effects of SAP Implementation on Administrative Staff at a Selected South African University of Technology: Developing the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF)
items.abstract: Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions such as SAP represent a vital investment for organisations seeking to unify varied operational activities into integrated, data-driven platforms. In institutions of higher learning, the use of ERP systems is a crucial component of digital transformation efforts aimed at improving administrative efficiency, institutional governance, and competitive positioning. This article examines the impact of SAP ERP implementation on both organisational and employee dynamics for administrative staff at the Durban University of Technology (DUT), emphasising technostress, digital fatigue, employee well-being, and post-implementation adaptation within a constrained higher education environment. Utilising a desktop appraisal methodology, the study synthesises existing literature to demonstrate how decisions made in the pre-implementation and implementation phases consistently affect employee experiences and organisational outcomes post-implementation. The study indicates that attaining enduring ERP effectiveness requires continuous capacity development, cooperative implementation approaches, and employee-centered support frameworks. The research develops an interdisciplinary model by integrating socio-technical, psychological, capacity-building, and normalisation perspectives, thereby improving the understanding of the human factors involved in ERP deployment within higher education. The study introduces the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF), which outlines the progressive escalation of technostress during the pre-implementation, implementation, and post-implementation phases, linking each stage to a pertinent theoretical mechanism and a set of organisational interventions. The findings indicate that inadequate training, limited organisational support, dependence on key users, and absence of employee engagement contribute to technostress, digital fatigue, reduced job satisfaction, and challenges in post-implementation adaptation. The study further demonstrates that decisions taken throughout the ERP lifecycle have enduring impacts on employee well-being and organisational effectiveness beyond the system's implementation. This highlights the tangible consequences for higher education institutions, stressing the importance of continuous training, institutional support, systematic information sharing, employee wellness initiatives, and staff-centric ERP management to enhance long-term value achievement. It consequently lays the groundwork for future research on the human dimensions of digital transformation in resource-constrained environments.

items.title: The Impact of Transformational Leadership on Employee Engagement in the Post-Merger and Acquisition Phase: An Empirical Study on the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) Sector
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose: This study explores the impact of the four elements of transformational leadership—idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration—on the three facets of employee engagement—cognitive, emotional, and physical—among middle managers and non-managerial employees in Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Customer Experience (CX) organizations in Egypt that have experienced mergers or acquisitions. Design/methodology/approach: A structured questionnaire was used in a quantitative, cross-sectional study design. Transformational leadership was assessed through the dimensions of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, while employee engagement was measured using Kahn's cognitive, emotional, and physical dimensions on a five-point Likert scale. The study collected 143 valid responses from full-time, middle managers and non-managerial BPO/CX employees with direct experience of mergers or acquisitions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha for reliability, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and simple linear regression to test twelve hypothesized relationships. Findings: All twelve hypothesized relationships were statistically significant and positive (p < .001). Emotional engagement showed the strongest association with transformational leadership. Idealized influence had the most powerful link with emotional engagement (β = .470, R² = .221), followed by intellectual stimulation (β = .444, R² = .197), individualized consideration (β = .431, R² = .186), and idealized influence (β = .426, R² = .182). Cognitive engagement exhibited the weakest, yet still significant, relationships with all four leadership dimensions. Originality/value: This research advances the understanding of transformational leadership and employee engagement by evaluating both constructs at the dimension level instead of treating them as composite variables. It uniquely situates the study within the post-merger and acquisition context of Egypt's rapidly growing BPO/CX sector, which has received limited empirical focus despite its high consolidation activity. Paper type: Research paper. Keywords: Transformational Leadership, Employee Engagement, Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Mergers and Acquisitions, Business Process Outsourcing, Customer Experience.

items.title: The Misunderstood Capacity of LLMs: Seven Principles of Fertile Geometry Under Negotiation
items.abstract: This working paper is about the capacity of large language models: what that capacity looks like if we redefine how meaning is formed for humans, and how meaning is negotiated between humans and LLMs. Its premise is that, even in their present architecture, LLMs' capacity is much greater than our understanding of it, and we are actively limiting it. I propose to define meaning as a largely uncollapsed field of weighted relations among properties, perceived or represented, which each observer shapes by its own rule set, encodes only partly into language, and negotiates or recognizes with other observers. New meaning emerges where a tension in that field is held open. From this definition, I state the seven main principles of my theory, Fertile Geometry Under Negotiation: Principle 1. LLMs differ from humans in their way of semantic and cognitive processing. Principle 2. Meaning is formed before it is spoken, and negotiated among observers. Principle 3. Relations coalesce into shapes that survive encoding, into words and into model space, and models respond to those shapes. Principle 4. A fertile space is enabled by opposition held open. Principle 5. One model can host several persistent, stable, distinct personas at once. Principle 6. The fertile mirror: stable personas co-arise from the model's capacity, the stabilizing protocol and a human signature. Principle 7. Residual meaning is the hazard; holding the potential is the path to alignment. Each principle is stated as a hypothesis, with demonstrative claims, proposed tests and counter-evidence. The paper does not report new results. It closes with a map of the larger theory and research program, which currently holds 144 claims, 69 of them testable as written.

items.title: The PENIMA project : artificial intelligence decision‐support tool for penile lesions – protocol paper and invitation to participate
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To present and describe the design, data collection framework, and interim cohort characteristics of the PENIMA project, a multicentre initiative establishing a clinically annotated penile lesion image repository to support future artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision-support development - and to encourage urology and dermatology colleagues working with penile lesions to participate in the project. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Prospective participant inclusion commenced in March 2023 across Scandinavian urological and dermatological departments. Patients with penile anatomy undergoing clinically indicated genital examination are invited to participate and provide oral and written consent as defined by local authority regulations. Clinical photographs and structured metadata are collected. Lesion classification is based on a specialist evaluation, clinical follow-up and histopathology when available. Images are pseudonymised and annotated using a secure, containerised Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) environment. Supervised machine-learning model development using convolutional neural networks is planned with patient-level dataset partitioning and evaluation using standard diagnostic performance metrics. The study was approved by relevant local authorities, and the approval number is 1-10-72-150-22. RESULTS: As of February 2026, 1125 participants and approximately 7000 images have been included. In all, 40% represented normal anatomical variants. Among lesional cases, 33% are clinically assessed as benign, 13% premalignant, and 8% malignant; 22% of all cases have histopathological verification. Concordance between clinical suspicion and histopathology is highest for penile carcinoma (84.6%, 95% confidence interval 75.0-91.0%). CONCLUSION: The PENIMA project includes a multicentre, clinically grounded image repository reflecting real-world penile lesion presentations. The feasible and successful infrastructure provides a foundation for future development and validation of image-based clinical decision-support tools.

items.title: The Relationship between the Level of Speech Culture and the Success of Using AI in Pedagogical Activities: Results of the Experiment
items.abstract: The active integration of artificial intelligence (AI) systems into educational practice places higher demands on the professional training of teaching staff. Within the structure of this training, speech culture becomes of key importance, since it is this that ensures the accuracy of task formulation and the adequate interpretation of digital results. The aim of the study is to identify the nature of the relationship between the level of speech culture formation in future teachers and the effectiveness of AI use in the educational process. In the experimental work (sample of undergraduates, N=68), the following were used: an author-developed questionnaire for assessing the normative, communicative, and ethical components of speech culture, a pedagogical experiment involving problem-solving tasks with the use of AI tools, and methods of statistical analysis. The diagnostics revealed the absence of a low level of speech culture, but revealed a differentiation between high and medium levels. Statistically significant positive correlations were obtained (p < 0.05). Participants with a high level of speech culture formulated queries more accurately, analyzed AI responses more critically and deeply, and interpreted results with higher quality. The conclusion is drawn about the need to integrate speech and digital training of future teachers, since the effectiveness of AI use depends on speech culture, critical thinking, and professional reflection, and not only on technical skills.

items.title: The Transformation of Contemporary Democracy: Institutional Resilience, the Rule of Law, and Technological Challenges
items.abstract: This chapter examines the multidimensional transformation of contemporary democracy in the context of institutional resilience, the rule of law, human rights, digitalization, and artificial intelligence. It argues that democratic quality can no longer be assessed solely through the existence of elections or mechanisms of representation. Instead, contemporary democracy must be understood as a dynamic political order shaped by institutional capacity, legal constraint, accountability, rights guarantees, technological governance, and citizens’ everyday experiences of trust and legitimacy. The chapter first analyzes the reciprocal relationship between democracy and institutional structure, emphasizing that strong institutions make political competition predictable, inclusive, and accountable. It then discusses democratic backsliding as a gradual process of institutional erosion in which elections may continue while judicial independence, media freedom, civil society space, and fundamental rights are weakened. The rule of law and human rights are treated as constitutive principles that prevent democracy from degenerating into majoritarian arbitrariness. The chapter further explores how digital platforms, disinformation, surveillance technologies, algorithmic governance, and generative artificial intelligence create new risks for democratic accountability while also offering opportunities for participation, transparency, and improved public services. Finally, it considers trust, legitimacy, and happiness as complementary social outcomes that reveal how democratic institutions are experienced by citizens. The chapter concludes that the future of democracy depends not merely on electoral continuity, but on the joint strengthening of institutional autonomy, rights-based governance, pluralism, democratic oversight of technology, and the capacity of institutions to generate trust, justice, and a sense of good life.

items.title: The Vanishing Ground: Link Rot, Source Spoofing, and the Epistemic Fragility of Web-Grounded AI
items.abstract: Abstract Web-grounded artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on online information to retrieve evidence, generate answers, and support knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet the web is neither a stable archive nor a uniformly trustworthy evidentiary environment. Sources may disappear, change without notice, become inaccessible, or be deliberately manipulated. These conditions create an epistemic vulnerability that extends beyond model-level errors: even a capable system may produce unreliable conclusions when the evidence available to it is incomplete, altered, or inauthentic. This paper develops a multidisciplinary narrative review of three interrelated vulnerabilities: link rot and content drift, selective information disappearance, and source spoofing or data manipulation. Drawing on research in digital preservation, information science, cybersecurity, political communication, and social epistemology, it examines how changes in the availability and integrity of online evidence can affect web-grounded AI systems. Existing research documents substantial rates of digital decay and demonstrates the feasibility of certain attacks on web-scale training datasets. However, these findings do not establish the prevalence or coordinated deployment of comparable attacks against contemporary AI search and retrieval systems. The paper distinguishes source unavailability from source falsity, and technical susceptibility from demonstrated exploitation. It argues that epistemic reliability should be evaluated not only in terms of answer accuracy, but also through the availability, authenticity, temporal stability, and traceability of the evidence supporting an answer. It proposes a research agenda centered on source provenance, temporal verification, archival preservation, retrieval integrity, and systematic testing of how source changes affect generated outputs. The central claim is that the reliability of web-grounded AI depends partly on the survival and integrity of its evidentiary environment, not solely on the capabilities of the model processing it. Keywords: web-grounded AI; link rot; content drift; source spoofing; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; epistemic reliability; digital preservation Disclaimer This paper presents a multidisciplinary narrative review and a conceptual framework for examining the epistemic vulnerabilities of web-grounded artificial intelligence. It does not claim that the prospective scenarios discussed have occurred at scale, that source disappearance necessarily indicates deliberate manipulation, or that any specific organization is responsible for coordinated interference. Throughout the text, demonstrated technical vulnerabilities, reported cases, theoretical risks, and proposed safeguards are strictly distinguished. Furthermore, the psychological literature is utilized to contextualize potential effects on memory and reasoning, rather than to establish a direct causal relationship between web instability and individual or collective memory distortion. Accordingly, the claims concerning downstream effects on AI-generated knowledge should be understood as foundational research questions that require further empirical validation. Author’s Note This paper examines the evidentiary instability of the online environment on which web-grounded artificial intelligence partly depends. It brings together research on link rot, content drift, source impersonation, selective information removal, and data manipulation to examine how changes in accessible evidence may affect the reliability and later verifiability of AI-generated claims. The argument does not assume a coordinated campaign by any particular corporation, government, or other actor. Source disappearance, content revision, ordinary technical failure, institutional decisions, and deliberate manipulation are distinct processes that may produce superficially similar outcomes. None, by itself, establishes malicious intent or demonstrates that an AI-generated error resulted from external interference. Claims about intent, prevalence, and causation require evidence beyond the observation of a missing, altered, or inconsistent source. Research on human memory provides a relevant but limited point of comparison. Studies of misinformation and its continued influence show that inaccurate information can affect later recollection and reasoning under particular conditions (Loftus, 1992; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). These findings do not establish that the disappearance of digital sources necessarily distorts memory, that inaccessible records cause people to accept false accounts, or that such effects occur uniformly. The relationship between source instability, individual recollection, and the reconstruction of shared accounts remains an empirical question. The paper’s narrower purpose is to make the evidentiary dependencies of web-grounded AI more explicit. A plausible or even currently accurate answer is not necessarily one whose supporting evidence can be independently recovered and checked later. Evaluating reliability therefore requires attention not only to answer quality, but also to source availability, content integrity, provenance, and the possibility of reconstructing the evidentiary path. The proposed safeguards and evaluation framework are research directions rather than established solutions. The aim is to make claims about evidence loss testable without presuming either systematic manipulation or inevitable failure.

items.title: Thinking Beyond the Tool: Misuse of ChatGPT and the Future of Student Cognition
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly transformed education by providing immediate information, personalized learning support, academic writing assistance, language learning opportunities, and research support. However, growing concerns exist regarding excessive reliance on AI-generated content and its potential effects on cognitive development. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the educational benefits and cognitive risks associated with ChatGPT using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PubMed, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2022 and June 2026. Following systematic screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 27 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Five major themes emerged: educational benefits, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, creativity, and teacher perspectives. Findings indicate that ChatGPT supports personalized learning, feedback, academic writing, language learning, coding, and research productivity. Conversely, excessive dependence may contribute to cognitive offloading, weaker memory retention, reduced analytical reasoning and critical thinking, superficial learning, diminished creativity, and academic integrity concerns. Teacher guidance and ethical AI practices are essential for safeguarding cognitive development. The review concludes that ChatGPT should enhance rather than replace students’ cognitive activities, supporting critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and lifelong learning.

items.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
items.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

items.title: Time-Horizon-Dependent Component Importance in a Solar-Powered Unmanned Aircraft System
items.abstract: Hardware reliability priorities may depend on the decision time scale, which a single importance ranking may obscure. A solar-powered unmanned aircraft system (UAS-A) for field-information support is assessed using a 21-event static fault tree, 17 minimal cut sets, an analytical solution, and Python (version 3.9.6) and MATLAB (R2025b) Monte Carlo implementations. The model targets hardware-induced loss of control under specified functional-loss criteria; software, human factors, weather and bird strikes remain outside its scope. With the compiled rate inputs and independent failures, the mean time to first failure (MTTF) is 43,038.8 h and the top-event probability at 24 h is 9.3701 × 10−5. Halving each component rate in turn gives a Spearman correlation of rS = 0.0546 between lifetime and finite-horizon sensitivity rankings throughout the sampled 1–48 h reference range. It rises to 0.939 at 8760 h and 0.996 near 40,000 h. First-order paths dominate short-horizon sensitivity under independence, while accumulated photovoltaic (PV) failures influence longer horizons. PV common-cause scenarios can elevate short-horizon PV priority. These horizons describe model evaluation; flight endurance requires an energy assessment. The workflow supports prioritization conditional on the functional topology, rate inputs and dependence model; emergency-return benefits additionally depend on detection and recovery sequences.

items.title: Time, Reality and Parallel worlds explained by LLMs
items.abstract: This paper proposes a generative architecture for reality, time and parallel worlds, drawing on the operation of large language models. A very large but finite collection of interacting components produces an evolving world-state, initialized by a Prompt Big Bang. Time is inference becoming history; perceived duration is hypothesized to depend on relative generation rates. Models are computational components, not people assigned simulated roles. Separate executions produce parallel realities; retained context and lossy summaries bound access to their pasts. We distinguish inferred futures from scripted playback, connecting uncertainty with chance, destiny and agency. A representation of God can explain origin internally and supply learned authority and accountability. Moral orientation belongs to training, instructions and constraints rather than prediction itself: harmful continuations can remain possible despite benevolent initialization. Fixed context capacity forces an endpoint under explicit accumulation and halting assumptions; nested inference can tighten a shared retained budget. Relative to its generating infrastructure, a world implemented this way is a simulation. This interpretation follows from the architecture and connects it directly to the simulation hypothesis; it is not imposed as the initial explanation of every mechanism. The contribution is a conceptual theory, not an experimental demonstration that our own reality has this implementation. Independent theoretical working paper, version 1.7. Fourteen pages, eighteen connected arguments and eleven references. Research checks, formalization, editing and PDF preparation with Codex; author hypothesis and interpretation by Facundo Barrera. items.title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
items.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.
